/email: Mail in your hive. A real email address, read and written from inside your hive, with every message kept sealed so only your key opens it.
Callout: Whoever runs the host keeps your mail and hands it to you sealed. They never hold the key that opens it.

How it works: Mail sent to your address reaches the host, which seals it to your key the moment it arrives and keeps only the sealed copy. Your hive asks the host for it with a request your key signs, and opens it on your device. When you write, your hive signs the message and the host sends it from your address.
New here? Get an address first. Before you trust a host with your mail, read What your host sees.
/email/get-an-address: Get an address. Your hive reads and writes mail at your own address, a few minutes after the host’s operator says yes.
For: You have a hive and want email in it. Someone runs a Hypercomb mail host, or you do.
You need: Your hive, open in a regular browser window. The host your mail will live on, as your Home Domain or on Your Network. A way to send that host’s operator a short message.

Step 1 -- Type `/mail` in the command line and press **Enter**. The mail desk opens over the page and asks each host your hive carries. Done when the desk says “This device’s key does not own a mailbox on any host you carry yet.”

Step 2 (optional) -- If the desk says your hive “carries none yet”, press **Open Your Network** and add the host your mail will live on. The host joins Your Network, and the mail desk asks it from then on. Done when the host’s name follows “Asked:” in the desk.

Step 3 -- Press **Copy key** and send the key to whoever runs the host. The key is the public half of the key your hive already holds. The secret half never leaves this device. Done when the button says “Copied”.

Step 4 -- When they say your address is ready, type `/mail` again. The desk opens your mailbox, and mail to your address is sealed to your key from then on. Done when your address shows at the top of the desk, above **Inbox** and **Sent**.
Callout: Run the host yourself? Then the desk says “You run <zone>: give this key an address.” Press **Give this key an address** and the form opens with your key already in it.
What it costs: Nothing in your hive. The host’s operator decides whether an address costs anything.
When you are done: You read and write mail from your hive. To know exactly what the host can and cannot see, read What your host sees.
Card: Read and write mail at an address on a host, from your hive. Free · 5 minutes
/email/give-addresses: Give addresses from your hive. You give, change and take back the addresses on the host you run from the mail desk, with nothing to redeploy after the first time.
For: You run a Hypercomb mail host. You want to hand out addresses without editing the host’s secret and redeploying.
You need: Your mail host, running as Run mail on your domain sets it up. A terminal in the mail Worker’s folder, signed in to your Cloudflare account. The hive you will give addresses from.
Part: Once: name yourself the operator

Step 1 -- Find your hive’s key. If this hive owns no mailbox yet, type `/mail` and press **Copy key**. If it already reads mail, your key is the one your host’s configuration lists for your address. Done when you hold 64 characters, each a digit or a letter from a to f.

Step 2 -- Run `npx wrangler secret put ADMIN_KEYS` in the mail Worker’s folder. Wrangler asks for the value: paste the key and press **Enter**. A second device’s key goes in the same value, after a comma. Done when wrangler says “Success! Uploaded secret ADMIN_KEYS”.
Step 3 -- Run `npx wrangler deploy` in the same folder. Wrangler uploads the Worker and lists the routes it answers on. Done when the list shows `<your zone>/mail/*`.
Step 4 -- Type `/mail` in your hive. The desk asks the host who you are, and the host now answers that you run it. Done when the desk shows a **Host** button.
Part: Give an address
Step 1 -- Press **Host**, then **Give an address**. A form opens under the addresses the host already holds. Done when the form asks for an **Address**, a **Zone** and a **Key**.

Step 2 -- Write the name before the @, pick the zone, and paste one to three public keys, one per line. **This device’s key** adds yours, and a name, a copy address and what each key may do are yours to choose. Done when at least one thing under **May** is ticked.

Step 3 -- Press **Save**. The host keeps the grant, and mail to the address is sealed to the keys you listed from then on. Done when the desk says the address “is given”, or “is yours now” when the key was yours.

Callout: Saving an address the host already lists replaces its whole record: its keys, its name and its copy address. The form fills in what the host holds, so press **Save** only when it shows everything you want kept.
Part: Change an address
Step 1 -- Press **Change** beside the address. The form opens holding what the host has for it. Done when the desk says “Changing <address>”.
Step 2 -- Change what you need and press **Save**. The host replaces the address’s record with what the form shows. Done when the desk says the address “is given”.
Part: Take an address back

Step 1 -- Press **Revoke** beside the address, then press it again. The first press asks “Revoke — press again”, and the second drops the grant. Done when the desk says “<address> is revoked. What already arrived stays as it is.”
Callout: An address the host’s own secret lists shows here marked “secret”. It is changed in the secret, never from the desk.
What it costs: Nothing beyond your host. A host takes at most 100 changes to its grants a day.

When you are done: Every address on your host is given, changed and taken back from this desk, and nothing is redeployed for it. To know what an operator key can and cannot do, read What your host sees.
Card: Give, change and take back addresses on your host from the mail desk. Free · 10 minutes

/email/run-a-host: Run mail on your domain. Your Cloudflare domain receives mail for its addresses, seals each message to its owner’s key, and sends as them, in about an hour.
For: You own a domain on Cloudflare and want mail at it, for yourself or for others. You are at home in a terminal.

You need: A domain whose DNS Cloudflare serves. Cloudflare’s Workers Paid plan, which Email Sending needs. Node, and a terminal signed in with `npx wrangler login`. The mail Worker, the folder src/hypercomb-relay/mail-worker in github.com/hypercomb/social. Your hive’s key, which the mail desk shows under **Copy key** while this hive owns no mailbox.

Step 1 -- Make the Worker yours in its wrangler.toml. Set routes to `<your zone>/mail/*`, and ALLOWED_ORIGINS to the addresses your people’s hives run at. Done when the file names your zone and no one else’s.

Step 2 -- Run `npx wrangler r2 bucket create hypercomb-mail` in the Worker’s folder. The bucket holds only sealed mail, and nothing in it is public. Done when `npx wrangler r2 bucket list` shows hypercomb-mail.

Step 3 -- Run `npx wrangler secret put ADMIN_KEYS` and paste your hive’s key. The host now takes grants from that key, so you give every address from your hive. Done when wrangler says “Success! Uploaded secret ADMIN_KEYS”.
Step 4 -- Run `npx wrangler deploy`. Wrangler uploads the Worker and lists the routes it answers on. Done when the list shows `<your zone>/mail/*`.

Step 5 -- Run `npx wrangler r2 bucket lifecycle add hypercomb-mail purge-trash trash/ --expire-days 30`. A delete only moves a message to the trash, so this rule is what empties it after 30 days. Done when `npx wrangler r2 bucket lifecycle list hypercomb-mail` shows purge-trash.

Step 6 -- In the Cloudflare dashboard, open Email Routing and set the rule for your addresses to **Send to a Worker**, choosing hypercomb-mail. Mail to those addresses now reaches the Worker, which seals it on arrival. Done when the rule shows hypercomb-mail as its action.

Step 7 -- Open Email Service, then Email Sending, then **Onboard Domain**, and follow it for your zone. Cloudflare adds the records that let the Worker send as your domain, including a strict DMARC rule. Done when your domain is listed under Email Sending.

Step 8 -- Give yourself an address from your hive, as Give addresses from your hive shows, then mail it from another account. The message arrives sealed to your key. Done when it is in **Inbox** when you type `/mail`.

Callout: The strict DMARC rule tells other mail servers to refuse mail sent as your domain that Cloudflare did not sign. Authorise any other service that sends as your domain, a newsletter tool for example, before you onboard.
What it costs: Cloudflare’s Workers Paid plan, at Cloudflare’s price. Mail you send to your own verified addresses does not count toward Cloudflare’s sending quota.
When you are done: Your domain receives and sends mail, and you give its addresses from your hive. Next, read Give addresses from your hive.
Card: Receive and send mail at your own Cloudflare domain, sealed to each owner’s key. Paid · 60 minutes
/email/what-the-host-sees: What your host sees. Exactly what the host that keeps your mail can see, what it cannot, and what an operator key can do.
For: You want to know who can read your mail before you trust a host with it.
Sealed: Every stored message is sealed to the keys listed for its address. The host keeps only the sealed copy, and only a listed key opens it.

What the host sees: When each message arrived, how large its sealed copy is, and its marks: read, flagged, hidden or ready to delete. The names of your addresses and folders. Your public key, on every request your hive signs, including the quiet check for new mail.

While a message moves: A message is plain inside Cloudflare while the Worker seals it on arrival, and while it sends what you write. That is true of receiving and sending any email. The Worker logs no content and no keys. Cloudflare can keep a preview of sent messages in the account’s activity log, which the operator can turn off.
Copies: A copy address gets each message unsealed, at the provider that holds it, for as long as it is kept. A message you save into your hive is unsealed there.

Operator keys: An operator key can list every address on the host with its keys, names and copy addresses. It can give an address to any key, so mail that arrives after that is sealed to that key too. It cannot open a message that was not sealed to it, change the host’s own secret, destroy mail, or send as an address it is not listed for.
A key that leaks: A leaked key can do everything the host lets it do at its address. Give each key only what it needs, so a recovery key only reads.
When you are done: You know what a host keeps and what it cannot. Next, read Get an address.
